summary: Applied capstone for place value to 10,000,000: learners choose and combine place-value tools — rounding to a stated place, ordering/comparing seven-digit and negative numbers, and reading/writing with placeholder zeros — within realistic multi-step problems (populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances). Core habit: estimate first by rounding, compute/compare exactly, then interpret the result back in context and judge whether an estimate is over or under.
misconceptions: Applying a rounding rule mechanically without checking the answer makes sense in context
Ordering by digit count or face value rather than aligned place value for seven-digit numbers
Mishandling negatives in context (ranking −900 m as shallower than −300 m)
Rounding to the wrong place for the purpose (nearest 10 when a million is asked for a headline)
Losing placeholder zeros when reading/writing the large numbers within a problem

activities.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool
steps: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
activities.insight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.

activities.title: Fluency check on the component skills
steps: Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and choose the correct result.
Order three negative trench depths (e.g. -4,000 m, -10,900 m, -7,200 m) from deepest to shallowest.
Estimate a total attendance (e.g. 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700) by rounding each to the nearest 100,000.
activities.insight: Each component place-value skill — rounding to a stated place, ordering negatives by position, estimating by rounding addends — can be executed accurately on its own.

activities.title: Framing contexts before computing
steps: Study a labelled population/depth chart or world map and tap or point to regions to reveal exact figures.
For each figure, state what you would round it to for a fair headline, and which figures you would keep exact for ranking.
Take on a journalist's brief: turn a set of exact figures into fair rounded headlines, then explain why the rounded version is appropriate for a headline but not for a precise ranking.
activities.insight: Deciding which place-value tool a situation calls for — and whether a rounded headline or an exact figure is appropriate — is itself part of the problem.

checkQuestion: Three tasks laid out on paper. (1) Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million. (2) Three ocean-trench readings are -4,000 m, -10,900 m and -7,200 m; order them from deepest to shallowest. (3) Estimate 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 by rounding each first.
